Drugmaker EMD Serono will reduce the cost of a common fertility medication under a deal with the Trump administration, President Donald Trump announced on Thursday, while also unveiling new federal guidance aimed at encouraging employers to offer fertility coverage.
The guidance will allow companies to offer fertility benefits separately from major medical insurance plans – similar to dental and vision cover – Trump said.
“We want to make it easier for all couples to have babies, raise children and start the families they have always dreamed about,” he added.

The Oval Office announcement provides a first look at how Trump plans to implement his executive order earlier this year aimed at reducing the cost of in vitro fertilisation (IVF) – a medical procedure that helps people facing infertility build their families.
However, it falls short of his campaign promise to make IVF treatment free.
It marks the third recent deal the administration has struck with pharmaceutical companies to cut drug prices.
EMD Serono's Gonal-f is among several drugs commonly used in IVF treatments – which involve using hormones to trigger ovulation and produce multiple eggs for fertilisation or freezing.
These medications can cost patients thousands of dollars per cycle – and many individuals undergo more than one cycle.

The White House and EMD Serono said the drug – along with all other IVF medications – will be available at a discount through TrumpRx, a government website where patients can purchase drugs directly from manufacturers.
The administration expects the website – which is planned to launch in 2026 – to reduce costs by bypassing intermediaries.
Trump also said the Food and Drug Administration will work with EMD Serono to expedite approval of another fertility drug available in Europe – called Pergoveris.
Thursday’s announcement follows Trump’s February executive order pledging to make IVF more affordable.
During his campaign last year, he promised that if elected, IVF treatment would be free.
The pledge came amid mounting pressure after his Supreme Court nominees contributed to overturning Roe v.
Wade – prompting GOP-led states to impose new restrictions that in some cases threatened IVF access by defining life as beginning at conception.
When asked on Thursday about conservatives with religious objections to IVF, Trump said he was unaware of those views.
Roger Shedlin, CEO of fertility and family-building benefits company WIN, welcomed the move as “steps in the right direction".
“Any initiative that addresses the cost of drugs will have a material positive impact on the overall cost of the fertility cycle,” he said.
Corinn O’Brien, 39, of Birmingham, Alabama, said any reduction in IVF costs would be “huge for families".
She underwent three rounds of IVF and gave birth to a daughter in June – with medication costs ranging from $1,000 to $5,000 per cycle.
Covering the entire IVF cycle, she said, “ultimately would be a game changer for families” – but reducing drug costs “is progress and is much appreciated”.
O’Brien added that it would be ideal if more employers offered fertility coverage – as “for many, this is their only chance to expand their family".
